claims.text: The ethanol-oxidation performance of the PGM nanoscale catalyst is governed by a high density of undercoordinated surface sites.
Undercoordinated surface sites provide high intrinsic catalytic activity.
Undercoordinated sites promote side reactions that reduce ethanol-oxidation selectivity.
Controlled thermal annealing reorganizes surface atoms and reduces the density of high-energy undercoordinated sites.
Annealing can reduce undercoordinated-site density without significantly changing the overall particle size.
Reducing undercoordinated-site density decreases the formation of intermediates that poison the catalyst.
Reducing undercoordinated-site density suppresses incomplete ethanol-oxidation products.
Annealing will increase selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation to CO2.
Annealing will improve catalyst durability over repeated reaction cycles.
Loss of highly active undercoordinated sites may modestly decrease reaction rate or peak current density.
The as-synthesized catalyst has a high density of undercoordinated surface atoms.
The as-synthesized baseline has good activity but lower selectivity and durability in ethanol oxidation.
The proposed mechanism should operate in acidic media at moderate potentials and temperatures.
At very high operating potentials or temperatures, undercoordinated-site density may cease to dominate reaction behavior.
The activity-selectivity-durability trade-off may depend on thermal-treatment details and on other defects or structural irregularities.
Acetaldehyde and acetic acid are partial ethanol-oxidation products that can be compared with CO2 in product analysis.

contradictions.description: The decrease in activity is described as only possible or potential, but the falsification rule treats an increase in activity without that trade-off as falsifying the hypothesis. An activity increase does not logically falsify a prediction that only conditionally anticipates a decrease.
